Amazon DynamoDB

Key-value/document storage organized around key-based access.

  • GameName + Version identifies a game version; querying GameName returns its versions. Category + GameName on a GSI supports category lookup.
  • A GSI only returns projected attributes; use ALL when the index must return every game attribute. GSI reads are eventually consistent.
  • TTL is a Number containing Unix seconds. Expiration is asynchronous cleanup; TTL deletions can appear in Streams. Filter expired data when required.

Decision boundary. Read-then-write can race. Use an atomic conditional write for a request ID, then coordinate status/results with business side effects.

CapacityBest starting clueWatch
On-demandVariable / uncertain request volumeHot keys and service quotas still apply
ProvisionedPredictable load; set read/write capacityThrottle if capacity is insufficient; consider Auto Scaling
Low-level PutItem: atomic request claim 
{
  "TableName": "RequestLedger",
  "Item": {
    "RequestId": {"S": "req-42"},
    "Status": {"S": "IN_PROGRESS"},
    "ExpiresAt": {"N": "1793318400"}
  },
  "ConditionExpression": "attribute_not_exists(RequestId)"
}

The key schema must make RequestId the primary key in this separate ledger. A successful claim does not prove the payment/write completed; persist outcomes and recover abandoned work. A String Version sorts lexically; use Number or suitable encoding for numeric ordering.

AWS reference: Global secondary indexes · TTL · Conditional expressions

Amazon SQS

Buffer work so consumers can process it independently.

  • Receive hides a message; DeleteMessage acknowledges success. Default visibility is 30 seconds, maximum 12 hours; duplicates still require idempotency.
  • PurgeQueue removes messages and keeps the queue. DeleteQueue removes both. RemovePermission edits queue-policy permission.
  • Choose queue type at creation; it cannot be converted later. Source and DLQ types must match. Queue tags are case-sensitive.

Decision boundary. VisibilityTimeout hides received work; DelaySeconds postpones initial availability; MessageRetentionPeriod limits retention. They are different clocks.

TypeDelivery / orderUse when
StandardAt least once; best-effort orderHigh throughput, order not required
FIFOOrdered within a message group; producer deduplicationOrdering/deduplication required; consumers remain idempotent
ReceiveMessage request (long polling) 
{
  "QueueUrl": "https://sqs.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com/123456789012/orders",
  "MaxNumberOfMessages": 10,
  "WaitTimeSeconds": 20,
  "VisibilityTimeout": 60
}

Backlog per worker = ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible / running workers. Target backlog = acceptable wait / average processing time. Apply target tracking to ECS with an appropriate task-count metric and a scale-from-zero strategy.

AWS reference: Visibility and acknowledgement · Queue attributes · Queue-based scaling

Kinesis Data Streams

Retain continuous events in shard lanes for independent, replayable reads.

  • A stream contains shards; shards contain records. Partition keys map records to a shard, where Kinesis assigns sequence numbers.
  • PutRecords batches records. HTTP 200 can include partial failures: inspect FailedRecordCount and each result; retry only failed entries with backoff and jitter.
  • ProvisionedThroughputExceededException indicates capacity/hot-key pressure; InternalFailure is a service-side record error. Preserve an application event ID for deduplication.

Decision boundary. Spreading partition keys can fix a hot shard. Increasing provisioned shards can add capacity; merging shards or sending more requests does not fix producer throttling.

Records flow through shards

A record is one event: a data blob + partition key, assigned a sequence number when accepted. A shard is an ordered lane of records with its own throughput capacity. A stream contains those lanes. A record belongs to one shard; the shard is not a batch sent to the consumer.

Example. Devices send readings continuously. Each record totals 4 KiB = 4,096 bytes, including its partition key, before base64 encoding. The sample below illustrates sustained provisioned capacity, without producer aggregation or burst allowances.

1 · Producer300 records/s × 4 KiB = 1.172 MiB/sPutRecord / PutRecords · IAM-authorized writes

↓ Partition-key hash → shard hash range

2 · AWS Kinesis stream · telemetry · one Region

Many keys are assumed evenly distributed in this model. With one shard, all records still enter that lane.

Shard 1Incoming: 300 records/s · 1.172 MiB/s
r1r2r3…→
Demand: 117% of byte budget · 30% of record budget · over capacity

↓ Read records from each shard; track progress per shard

3 · Consumer applicationProcess accepted readings → update dashboard / store resultsGetRecords polling or enhanced fan-out · IAM-authorized reads

300 records/s exceed one shard's sustained byte budget. Some writes can be throttled; retry failed records with backoff and jitter.

Per shard: min(1,000 records/s, 1,024 KiB/s ÷ 4 KiB) = 256 records/s. At 300 records/s, at least 2 evenly loaded shards are needed before headroom.

Two limits, one lane. Each shard supports sustained writes up to 1 MiB/s and 1,000 records/s; whichever is reached first limits you. At 4 KiB, bytes win. With 512-byte records, the record-count limit would win. These are rates, not the shard's total storage size.

Reading is independent. Shared-throughput consumers share up to 2 MiB/s per shard; enhanced fan-out provides up to 2 MiB/s per shard per registered consumer. Reading does not delete records. Retention controls replay; there is no global order across shards. PutRecords retries can also change producer event order.

Capacity ≠ retention. The lane continues accepting records over time; it does not fill at 1 MiB and move to the next shard. Control-plane scaling changes the shard layout; data-plane calls write/read records. On-demand manages capacity for you, but a hot partition key still needs attention.

Capacity modeWho manages capacityWatch
ProvisionedYou set shard countPer-shard throughput / hot partition keys
On-demandService scales stream capacityScaling boundaries, hot keys and quotas still apply
PutRecords response: retry the second input record 
{
  "FailedRecordCount": 1,
  "Records": [
    {"SequenceNumber": "101", "ShardId": "shardId-000000000000"},
    {"ErrorCode": "ProvisionedThroughputExceededException",
     "ErrorMessage": "Rate exceeded"}
  ]
}

Results align with request order. PutRecords does not guarantee ordering across successful and retried records. Reducing readers does not directly fix producer-side write throttling.

AWS reference: Producer API and partial failures · Streams, records & shards · Sustained shard capacity · Current quotas & large-record limits · Enhanced fan-out

Amazon ECS

Orchestrate container tasks and services; choose their compute separately.

  • ECS schedules tasks/services. A task definition is the container blueprint; a service maintains the desired tasks. EC2 and Fargate are distinct capacity choices.
  • Task-local ephemeral/bind-mount data is suitable for temporary files. EC2 host volumes depend on host lifecycle.
  • EFS provides persistent shared network files for supported ECS/Fargate tasks across AZs. Configure mount targets, NFS access and file permissions.

Decision boundary. A local volume is not a shared cross-AZ filesystem. Fargate EFS support requires a supported Linux platform; do not assume every OS/launch mode supports it.

NeedChooseLifecycle
Temporary task filesEphemeral storage / supported bind mountTask/host dependent
Shared persistent filesEFSIndependent of task replacement
Host configuration controlECS on EC2You manage host capacity
Managed container computeFargateTask CPU/memory allocation
Task-definition storage excerpt 
{
  "volumes": [{
    "name": "shared",
    "efsVolumeConfiguration": {
      "fileSystemId": "fs-example",
      "transitEncryption": "ENABLED"
    }
  }],
  "containerDefinitions": [{
    "name": "worker", "image": "example/worker:1",
    "mountPoints": [{"sourceVolume": "shared", "containerPath": "/data"}]
  }]
}

The excerpt omits task roles, CPU/memory, networking and other required task settings. Add an EFS access point/IAM authorization where needed; a mount declaration alone does not grant access.

AWS reference: ECS concepts and capacity · EFS with ECS / Fargate

AWS Fargate

Supply managed compute capacity for containers without managing EC2 hosts.

  • For ECS, define the image, task CPU/memory, networking and roles; Fargate supplies isolated task compute.
  • ECS still schedules tasks/services. You continue to own the container, IAM permissions, security groups and application behavior.
  • Task-local storage is ephemeral. Use supported EFS integration when tasks need shared persistent files.

Decision boundary. Fargate is container compute; ECS is orchestration. Fargate does not build images or define infrastructure templates. Choose self-managed EC2 capacity when host-level requirements demand it.

Capacity choiceTrade-off
FargateManaged task compute; supported CPU/memory/platform combinations
Fargate SpotDiscounted interruptible capacity; design interruption-tolerant work
ECS on EC2Host control and host-capacity responsibilities
Fargate task-definition excerpt 
{
  "family": "orders-worker",
  "requiresCompatibilities": ["FARGATE"],
  "networkMode": "awsvpc",
  "cpu": "256",
  "memory": "512",
  "containerDefinitions": [{
    "name": "worker",
    "image": "123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/orders:1",
    "essential": true
  }]
}

Add task execution/application roles and the network configuration when launching tasks. The task execution role covers supported agent actions such as image pulls; the task role grants permissions to application code.

AWS reference: Fargate with ECS

Amazon RDS

Managed relational databases with SQL and transactions.

  • Read replicas asynchronously copy data; the application must send reads to replica endpoints. Expect possible replication lag.
  • A traditional Multi-AZ DB instance has a standby for failover, not reads.
  • A Multi-AZ DB cluster has readable standby DB instances; engine/configuration support matters.

Decision boundary. Read load points to replicas; failover points to Multi-AZ; repeated reusable results may point to a cache. These choices can coexist.

OptionMain purposeReadable secondary?
Read replicaScale readsYes; async replication lag
Multi-AZ DB instanceAvailability / failoverNo
Multi-AZ DB clusterAvailability + read capacityYes, supported cluster engines
Route reads explicitly 
# Application routing, not an AWS API payload
write_connection = connect(primary_endpoint)
report_connection = connect(read_replica_endpoint)
# Use the primary for reads that require the latest committed value.

AWS reference: Multi-AZ instance vs cluster · Read replica operation

Amazon ElastiCache

Keep frequently reused data in memory.

  • Valkey, Redis OSS and Memcached support low-latency cached access; choose engine capabilities deliberately.
  • A cache hit can reduce database work. A miss still needs a source-of-truth lookup.
  • Use expiry and invalidation to manage staleness. Memcached is not a durable primary database.

Decision boundary. A cache endpoint does not execute relational SQL in place of RDS. Cache-aside requires application logic and a key design.

DeploymentOperational choicePricing shape
ServerlessService manages cache capacityData storage + request/compute usage
Node-basedSelect node types/count/topologyProvisioned nodes; reservation options where supported
Cache-aside pseudocode 
key = f"game:{name}:{version}"
value = cache.get(key)
if value is None:
    value = database.load_game(name, version)
    cache.set(key, serialize(value), ttl=60)
return deserialize_if_needed(value)

AWS reference: Engine and deployment options

IAM, STS & Access Analyzer

Establish AWS trust and evaluate permissions.

  • Identity policies grant actions; supported resource policies grant access to resources. A role trust policy says who may assume it; STS issues temporary credentials.
  • Permissions boundaries and SCPs limit applicable permissions; they do not grant actions. An explicit applicable deny overrides an allow.
  • Access Analyzer finds supported external/unused access and validates policies. Policy variables can scope reusable access, e.g. an IAM user’s own S3 prefix.

Decision boundary. Trusting an identity does not authorize every resource. ${aws:username} is for IAM users and is not generally present for role sessions; use suitable principal tags/identity variables.

IAM-user prefix policy (illustrative) 
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:GetObject",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::study-home/${aws:username}/*"
  }]
}

Billing-console access can require the account root user to Activate IAM Access plus appropriate IAM permissions. SCPs govern member-account principals within their documented scope; they are not a universal policy attached to every possible caller.

AWS reference: Policy evaluation · Access Analyzer · Policy variables · Billing console activation

Security groups & NACLs

Filter network traffic at two different boundaries.

  • Security groups attach to network interfaces and are stateful: allowed traffic automatically permits its response.
  • NACLs operate at subnet boundaries and are stateless: allow the required request and return traffic, including ephemeral ports.
  • Check routes, security groups, NACLs, listener and target health separately when diagnosing connectivity.

Decision boundary. Network reachability does not authenticate a user or grant an IAM action. Security groups use allow rules only; NACLs support allow and deny.

ControlScopeRulesResponse traffic
Security groupNetwork interfaceAllow onlyStateful
NACLSubnet boundaryAllow + deny; rule orderStateless; explicit return rules
Request path to inspect 
client --HTTPS 443--> public ALB
ALB security group --app port--> private target security group
subnet NACL: allow request + return-port traffic both ways

AWS reference: VPC security controls · Security group / NACL comparison

Amazon S3 encryption

Store objects; enforce the encryption contract at upload.

  • New S3 uploads are encrypted by default. SSE-S3 uses AES256; SSE-KMS uses aws:kms in the encryption request header.
  • Default bucket encryption chooses storage encryption even when the client omits a header.
  • A bucket policy can require an explicit mode/key. Missing-header checks and incorrect-value checks express different requirements.

Decision boundary. Requiring a request header rejects clients that rely on bucket defaults. Requiring aws:kms alone does not pin a particular KMS key; validate its key ID/ARN when required.

ModeHeader valueKeys / costs
SSE-S3AES256S3 manages keys; baseline encryption
SSE-KMSaws:kmsKMS policy/use permissions; KMS charges may apply
Explicit SSE-KMS header enforcement policy 
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Sid": "DenyMissingEncryptionHeader",
    "Effect": "Deny", "Principal": "*",
    "Action": "s3:PutObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::study-bucket/*",
    "Condition": {"Null": {"s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption": "true"}}
  }, {
    "Sid": "DenyWrongEncryptionMode",
    "Effect": "Deny", "Principal": "*",
    "Action": "s3:PutObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::study-bucket/*",
    "Condition": {"StringNotEquals": {"s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption": "aws:kms"}}
  }]
}

Illustrative bucket name. This narrow policy shows request enforcement, not complete bucket access. KMS upload/download permissions and bucket policies must also allow the intended principal.

AWS reference: SSE-KMS and enforcement

AWS KMS

Control cryptographic keys and cryptographic operations.

  • Use a KMS key directly for supported small payloads; use envelope encryption for larger application data.
  • GenerateDataKey returns plaintext and encrypted copies of a data key. Encrypt data locally, discard plaintext key, store the encrypted key with ciphertext.
  • Normal crypto calls do not return the underlying KMS key material. Rotation support depends on key type/origin; rotating key material is not recreating a key per request.

Decision boundary. Encryption does not replace authorization. A principal needs the relevant service access and KMS key-use authorization; cross-account use requires compatible policies.

Large-payload encryption pseudocode 
# Envelope encryption, conceptual flow
plain_key, encrypted_key = kms.generate_data_key(key_id, key_spec="AES_256")
ciphertext = authenticated_encrypt(plain_key, document)
securely_discard(plain_key)
store(ciphertext, encrypted_key)
# Later: KMS Decrypt(encrypted_key) → data key → decrypt document.

AWS reference: Envelope encryption · Data keys · Key rotation

Amazon Cognito

Authenticate application users; federate them into AWS access when needed.

  • User pools provide a user directory/federation and issue ID/access JWTs plus refresh tokens.
  • Identity pools exchange supported identities for temporary AWS credentials, including narrowly scoped guest access when enabled.
  • API Gateway can authorize with Cognito tokens; a Lambda authorizer supports custom token validation/rules. HTTP APIs have native JWT authorizers.

Decision boundary. A user-pool JWT is not an access key. A browser may call your API with a bearer token, while the backend calls AWS with its own role credentials.

RequirementChooseWhat comes out
Sign in app usersUser pool (+ external IdP if needed)ID/access JWT + refresh token
Direct AWS resource accessIdentity pool + IAM roleTemporary access key/secret/session token
Custom API rulesLambda authorizerAPI authorization result
AWS API invocationAuthorized IAM principal + SigV4Signed request
Different credential contracts 
# Authenticated application → protected API
Authorization: Bearer <access-token-JWT>

# Direct AWS SDK access uses temporary credentials instead
{"AccessKeyId":"<temporary-id>",
 "SecretKey":"<temporary-secret>",
 "SessionToken":"<session-token>",
 "Expiration":"<expiry>"}

Validate token signature, issuer, audience/client binding, token_use and expiry; apply required scopes and record/tenant rules. User and identity pools can be combined. Never place a secret credential in a public client bundle.

AWS reference: User pools · Identity pools and AWS credentials · API authorizer choices

Secrets Manager & Parameter Store

Separate credentials from application configuration.

  • Secrets Manager stores secrets and supports automatic rotation through service-managed integrations or Lambda workflows, depending on secret type.
  • Parameter Store stores named configuration, versions and encrypted SecureString values; it has no equivalent native database-password rotation workflow.
  • Grant runtime roles narrow read/decrypt access. Retrieve and cache values appropriately; do not embed secrets in code or logs.

Decision boundary. Rotating RDS credentials points to Secrets Manager. An expiration notification/parameter policy is not a password-rotation implementation.

OptionUsePricing / lifecycle
Secrets ManagerCredentials + rotationPer secret + API use; integration-specific rotation
Parameter Store StandardSmall static configStandard storage free; throughput options may bill
Parameter Store AdvancedLarger values, policies, more scalePer advanced parameter + API/throughput charges
AppConfigValidated configuration / feature rolloutSeparate controlled deployment capability
Runtime retrieval commands 
# AWS CLI; never print this result in application logs
aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id prod/orders/db
aws ssm get-parameter --name /prod/orders/endpoint
aws ssm get-parameter --name /prod/orders/token --with-decryption

SecureString needs appropriate KMS permissions. Parameter Store can reference a Secrets Manager secret as a pass-through; the rotation capability still belongs to Secrets Manager.

AWS reference: Parameter Store comparison · Secrets rotation

CloudWatch, CloudTrail & tracing

Choose evidence that can actually answer the question.

  • CloudWatch metrics show aggregate demand/latency/errors; Logs hold application events when configured.
  • ALB access logs show client IP, path, timing and status. CloudTrail shows supported AWS API/account events, not every HTTP request.
  • Trace IDs correlate requests; distributed tracing reveals downstream latency when the application/services are instrumented.

Decision boundary. Check target health settings and reachability before scaling an unhealthy target. Adding capacity does not fix a wrong health-check path or denied request.

Investigation sequence 
symptom: HTTP 5xx increased after deployment
1. CloudWatch: when, how many, ALB or target errors?
2. ALB access logs: which path / target / status / timing?
3. Trace + app log: which dependency failed?
4. CloudTrail: who changed the configuration?

CloudTrail data events are service/operation-specific and often require explicit enablement. They do not replace application access logs. Avoid sensitive credentials/payloads in diagnostic logs.

AWS reference: ALB request evidence · CloudTrail event types · CloudWatch concepts

AWS CodePipeline

Coordinate the stages that turn a source revision into a release.

  • Source, build/test, approval and deploy actions form an orchestrated delivery workflow.
  • CodePipeline passes artifacts and invokes action providers. CodeBuild runs build commands; CloudFormation and CodeDeploy perform their respective deployment actions.
  • A pipeline service role and action-specific permissions authorize delivery. They are separate from the runtime application role.

Decision boundary. A successful pipeline action proves that action succeeded; verify which artifact, configuration and route are actually serving production.

TypeChoiceCost comparison
V1Standard pipeline/stage/action structureCompare active-pipeline pricing
V2Adds release-safety and trigger configurationCompare action-execution pricing; see current rates
Pipeline build-stage excerpt 
{
  "name": "BuildAndTest",
  "actions": [{
    "name": "Build",
    "actionTypeId": {
      "category": "Build", "owner": "AWS",
      "provider": "CodeBuild", "version": "1"
    },
    "configuration": {"ProjectName": "orders-build"},
    "inputArtifacts": [{"name": "SourceOutput"}],
    "outputArtifacts": [{"name": "BuildOutput"}]
  }]
}

This is one stage, not a complete CreatePipeline request. Source connection, roles, artifact storage and deploy actions are configured elsewhere.

AWS reference: Pipeline responsibility · Pipeline types · Current pricing

AWS CodeBuild

Run build/test commands and produce a deployable artifact.

  • The buildspec defines phases, commands and artifact output. A managed build environment runs those commands.
  • Package Lambda ZIPs or container images for the target runtime. S3 stores build artifacts; ECR stores container images; CodeArtifact stores software packages.
  • Run unit/integration tests and inspect their results. Amazon Q Developer can assist with code and tests; developers still review and validate the result.

Decision boundary. Compiling code is not deploying it. A passing unit test does not prove the production integration, IAM permissions or active route are correct.

Compute choiceStarting clueWatch
EC2 on-demandFlexible build environment without a standing fleetImage, architecture and resource requirements
EC2 reserved capacityManage a fleet for predictable build demandCapacity commitment and utilization
Lambda computeFast startup for supported buildsSupported runtimes, features and duration limits
buildspec.yml for an illustrative Python project 
version: 0.2
phases:
  install:
    commands:
      - pip install -r requirements.txt -t package/
  build:
    commands:
      - python -m pytest tests/
      - cp app.py package/
      - cd package && zip -r ../function.zip .
artifacts:
  files:
    - function.zip

The example assumes a suitable Linux build image with pytest and zip available, and the named project files. Pin dependencies and select compute from measured build requirements.

AWS reference: CodeBuild role · Compute modes · Buildspec contract · Q Developer in exam scope

AWS CodeDeploy

Roll out an application revision using a platform-specific deployment contract.

  • Supports EC2/on-premises, Lambda and ECS deployment platforms.
  • The AppSpec describes target resources and lifecycle hooks. Deployment configuration controls rollout; configured alarms/hooks support validation and recovery.
  • Lambda traffic shifting moves an alias between published versions. ECS blue/green shifts service traffic; EC2 deployments can update in place or use replacements.

Decision boundary. CloudFormation manages declared resources and can deploy application resources/code. CodeDeploy specializes in rollout, hooks and traffic shifting; it does not build the artifact.

TargetRelease unitKey distinction
LambdaPublished versions + aliasCanary/linear/all-at-once traffic configuration
ECSTask definition + target serviceBlue/green task sets and traffic routing
EC2/on-premisesApplication revision + hooksIn-place or supported blue/green deployment
Lambda AppSpec excerpt 
version: 0.0
Resources:
  - OrdersFunction:
      Type: AWS::Lambda::Function
      Properties:
        Name: orders
        Alias: prod
        CurrentVersion: '1'
        TargetVersion: '2'

The deployment group, service role, traffic policy, alarms and optional hooks are configured separately. Verify the actual alias/target and business health before considering a release complete.

AWS reference: Platforms and rollout · AppSpec examples

EventBridge & SNS

Route events or fan a publication out to independent consumers.

  • EventBridge connects event sources to matching targets; bus and feature selection determine supported routing/replay behavior.
  • SNS publishes to topics and pushes to subscribed endpoints. An SNS-to-SQS fanout gives consumers independent queues.
  • A consumer needs its own authorization, retry and idempotency handling. An accepted publication does not prove the business work completed.

Decision boundary. A router or topic does not retain the progress of a multi-step business workflow. A queue buffers pending work; a state machine coordinates steps.

NeedStarting choice
Route by event content / sourceEventBridge bus and matching target configuration
Publish once to multiple subscribersSNS topic; optional subscription filters
Independent backlogs per consumerSNS/EventBridge delivery to separate SQS queues
Durable progress across ordered stepsStep Functions workflow
EventBridge PutEvents example 
{
  "Entries": [{
    "Source": "com.example.orders",
    "DetailType": "OrderAccepted",
    "Detail": "{\"orderId\":\"o-42\",\"requestId\":\"r-42\"}",
    "EventBusName": "orders"
  }]
}

This illustrates the JSON PutEvents contract for a compatible configured bus. Check per-entry publication results and the exact bus mode; current EventBridge bus types have different feature contracts.

AWS reference: EventBridge capabilities · SNS fanout

AWS Step Functions

Coordinate application steps with explicit state and failure handling.

  • A state machine expresses service calls, branching and supported waits/retries/catches.
  • Lambda or ECS executes task code; Step Functions retains workflow progress. The workflow execution role needs target-service permissions.
  • Choose workflow type from duration, integration and execution-semantics requirements; make external side effects idempotent.

Decision boundary. CodePipeline coordinates software delivery; Step Functions coordinates application/business work. A workflow is optional when one handler or independent consumers suffice.

TypePrimary boundaryBilling shape
StandardDurable execution, up to one year; supported callback/job integrationsState transitions
ExpressShort high-volume execution, up to five minutes; integration differencesExecutions + duration/memory
Amazon States Language: one application task 
{
  "StartAt": "RecordOrder",
  "States": {
    "RecordOrder": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke",
      "Parameters": {"FunctionName": "orders", "Payload.$": "$"},
      "End": true
    }
  }
}

The sample omits retries and business error handling. Workflow execution semantics do not make an external payment exactly once; plan for uncertain task outcomes and replay.

AWS reference: Workflow types · Lambda integration

AWS AppConfig

Validate and gradually deploy application configuration or feature flags.

  • Separate configuration data from the code artifact so supported behavior can change without rebuilding code.
  • Validators check configuration; deployment strategies control rollout. Configured monitoring can trigger recovery.
  • Applications retrieve configuration through supported agents/APIs. Parameter Store and Secrets Manager have different storage/rotation responsibilities.

Decision boundary. Creating a configuration version does not make every running process use it. Verify deployment, environment and application retrieval/cache behavior.

StartDeployment: illustrative identifiers 
{
  "ApplicationId": "a1b2c3d",
  "EnvironmentId": "e1f2g3h",
  "ConfigurationProfileId": "p1q2r3s",
  "ConfigurationVersion": "7",
  "DeploymentStrategyId": "d1e2f3g"
}

The application, environment, profile, validators, deployment strategy and monitoring must already be configured. Current pricing depends on retrieval/deployment usage; check AWS rates for the chosen retrieval pattern.

AWS reference: Configuration rollout · StartDeployment contract
